text:
Single-negative BCE is a plausible contributor to weak ranking, but Electronics-specific causation remains untested. [gSASRec (2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf) identifies sampling-induced overconfidence and improves SASRec using multiple negatives plus generalized BCE; recommended defaults are 128–256 negatives and calibration t=0.75. [Loss analysis (2024, revised 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770) shows single-negative categorical cross-entropy equals BPR, so switching between those objectives alone adds no distinction. [Scalable Cross-Entropy (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18721) supports CE-style training with informative candidate subsets when full-catalog logits exceed memory limits.

Hardness requires caution with sparse implicit feedback: unobserved items can be relevant. [CATS (2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) proposes adaptive cluster-based sampling to balance informative negatives against potential false negatives; its same-cluster relevance assumption is a heuristic, not observed preference. A [controlled sampling study (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds dataset-dependent tradeoffs: uniform sampling favors head items, while popularity-based negatives can improve balance while lowering overall accuracy. Neither aggressive hard mining nor popularity sampling guarantees better top-k results.

Practical experiment proposal: hold architecture and splits fixed; compare single-negative BCE, multi-negative BCE, gBCE, and multi-negative sampled softmax. Then test a modest mixture of uniform and semi-hard negatives, masking padding, targets, and known training positives; downweight uncertain negatives rather than assuming all high-scoring unseen items are irrelevant. These are hypotheses, not measured gains. Select exclusively by unchanged four-category macro validation HR@10 with pinned candidates/seeds; inspect Electronics margins and per-category HR diagnostically, and account for each trial’s GPU cost.
